one_liner: Fully managed F# binary analysis framework whose x86/x86-64 front-end out-ran Capstone.NET about 4.4x in its authors' print-every-instruction harness.
what_it_does: B2R2 parses, disassembles, assembles and lifts machine code to its LowUIR intermediate representation and recovers control-flow graphs, for x86/x86-64, ARMv7, AArch64, MIPS, RISC-V, PPC, SPARC, S390, SH4, AVR, EVM, WASM, CIL and more, reading ELF, PE, Mach-O and WebAssembly files. It is a .NET library: you load bytes with BinHandle.LoadRawImage (or a file), create a LiftingUnit and call ParseInstruction/TryParseInstruction, DisasmInstruction or LiftInstruction. It is not an API replacement for Capstone; the instruction objects, operand model and disassembly syntax differ.
how_it_is_fast: The x86 parser checks prefixes with a bitmap per high-3-bit group, then dispatches into straight-line per-opcode code that the IntelParserGen generator writes at build time from the instruction table (LegacyOpcodeMap/VEXOpcodeMap), so nothing is looked up at parse time. Since PR #590 (September 2026) operands are value types stored inside the instruction object, cutting per-instruction allocations from three to one; the PR reports this as about 1.4x faster than the previous table-driven parser on the same blobs (relative numbers only). The parser works on ReadOnlySpan<byte> slices of the image, with no native code or P/Invoke.
when_to_use: You are already on .NET (F# or C#) and want x86/x86-64 decoding plus lifting to an IR and CFG recovery in one fully managed package, with no native Capstone binaries to ship.
You need one decoder API across many ISAs (x86, ARM, MIPS, RISC-V, PPC, SPARC, EVM, WASM and others) inside a .NET analysis tool.
You are replacing Capstone.NET or the Capstone Python bindings in a .NET or scripted pipeline where per-instruction marshalling through a wrapper is the bottleneck.
You want to parallelise lifting or CFG recovery: the API supports it by creating one LiftingUnit per thread.
when_not_to_use: From C or C++: it is an F#/.NET assembly with no C API, so it needs a hosted CLR or a separate process; native Zydis, bddisasm, XED or iced (Rust) are the direct options.
When raw x86 decode speed is all you need: in the same harness the C# build of iced was faster (15.737 s vs 17.748 s average), and iced also ships an encoder and a Rust crate.

Linear sweeps over data-heavy or misaligned bytes: every undecodable position goes through a .NET exception (raised in the parser, re-raised by LiftingUnit, caught by TryParseInstruction), which is far slower than a normal decode.

When you need a stable API: 0.x releases rename packages and types (B2R2.FrontEnd.BinInterface and BinHandle.TryParseInstr used by the 2021 benchmark are gone; the current package is B2R2.FrontEnd.API on net10.0).
When you need Capstone's exact output: disassembly syntax and operand formatting differ, and decoding bugs are still being fixed (issues #279 SHA family, #634 ARMv7).

integration.dependencies: the .NET 10 runtime and FSharp.Core; the core library has no other external dependencies (FParsec, FSharp.Compiler.Service, BenchmarkDotNet and Avalonia.FuncUI are used only by optional tools)
integration.min_toolchain: .NET 10 SDK (net10.0 target, FSharp.Core 10.0.103 pinned) for the current 0.10.1 release; the 2021 benchmark used B2R2 0.5.0 on net5.0
integration.platforms: any OS .NET supports (Linux, macOS, Windows); decodes x86, x86-64, ARMv7, AArch64, MIPS32/64, RISC-V 32/64, PPC32/64, SPARC, S390/S390x, SH4, M68K, Alpha, PA-RISC, AVR, TMS320C6000, EVM, eBPF, WASM, CIL and Python bytecode
integration.thread_safety: A LiftingUnit is per-thread: the docs say lifting in parallel needs multiple lifting units; a global mutable variable in the Intel front-end was removed in issue #87 (2025).

gotchas: Harness flaw: every tool's timed loop prints each instruction with Console.WriteLine (autoflushed .NET console, or print in Python), so the table measures output more than decoding. B2R2 ran blob_x86 (78,369,750 bytes) at about 2.8 MB/s, iced at 3.1 MB/s and Capstone.NET at 0.61 MB/s (derived from page data). That is roughly 10x below the native decode+format rates in disas-bench (Capstone 27.5 MB/s, different hardware), and iced, B2R2 and SharpDisasm sit within 16% of each other, which fits a shared output floor. The 4.4x figure is not a decoder-speed ratio.

Unequal work in the harness: Capstone runs with skipdata, so undecodable bytes are formatted and printed as .byte lines, while the B2R2 harness silently advances one byte; the Python harness prints address and operands but no mnemonic. Capstone.NET's timed region also includes creating the disassembler, while B2R2's file load is outside its timer. Capstone.NET's wrapper (current 9ee1/Capstone.NET source; 2.0.2 not checked) pins the whole input array with GCHandle.Alloc on every Iterate step and builds a managed instruction object with marshalled strings, so the baseline is a binding, not native Capstone 4.x.

Stale numbers: they are for B2R2 0.5.0 (comparison repo last updated 2021-10-23). The Intel parser has since been rewritten twice: first table-driven, then generated per-opcode code (PR #590). The harness no longer builds against current B2R2, because the BinInterface package and the TryParseInstr API are gone.

Undecodable bytes cost exceptions: Parser.Parse wraps all errors into ParsingFailureException, LiftingUnit.parse re-raises it, and TryParseInstruction catches it, so a Result-returning call still throws internally on every bad byte.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick B2R2 over iced, Zydis, bddisasm or XED only when you want decoding, lifting to an IR and CFG recovery for many ISAs in one managed .NET package. For pure x86 decode/format speed, iced (C# or Rust) beat it in the authors' own table, and Zydis or bddisasm are the native C choices with independent disas-bench numbers.
verified_claims_summary: In the B2R2 authors' DisasmComparison repo (B2R2 0.5.0 on net5.0; CPU, OS and .NET SDK not stated; mean of 10 runs), linear-sweep disassembly of three BAR'19 blobs, with each instruction printed inside the timer, took 28.3/24.3/0.63 s against 127.8/106.4/2.25 s for Capstone.NET (Gee.External.Capstone 2.0.2 over Capstone 4.x) and 132.7/111.6/2.22 s for the Capstone Python bindings. That is about 4.4x on average against Capstone.NET, while C# iced was faster still (15.7 s average). The times are dominated by console output and the tools do unequal work, so this is not a native Capstone comparison.
status_note: Very active (0.10.1 released 2026-06-17, commits through 2026-10-11, parser speed work in September 2026) and MIT-licensed, but a 0.x .NET library with frequent API renames, not callable from C++ without hosting the CLR; the only benchmark is a five-year-old first-party run.
